data.title: Stocks to watch: Jardine Matheson, Riverstone, Deluge
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Wednesday (Nov 18):

Jardine Matheson: The Hong Kong-based conglomerate expects to post a 2026 dividend of at least US$2.50 per share, amid “strong performance” for the third quarter ended Sep 30. This comes after Jardine Matheson raised its full-year profit guidance in October to between US$5.50 and US$5.65 per share on an underlying basis, from the previous guidance of US$5.33 per share. For Q3, its Indonesian unit Astra International’s underlying net profit rose 11 per cent. Shares of Jardine Matheson closed 1 per cent or US$0.62 lower at US$59.15 on Tuesday, before the news.

Riverstone : The glove maker posted a 34.7 per cent rise in net profit to RM70.1 million (US$17.1 million) for the third quarter ended September. Riverstone’s Q3 revenue rose 27.3 per cent to RM315.1 million, marking the group’s highest quarterly revenue in over three years. It also announced that CEO Wong Teek Son will step down on Dec 1, to be succeeded by Chong Chu Mee. Riverstone shares closed 2.1 per cent or S$0.015 higher at S$0.745 on Tuesday, before the results.

Deluge : The fire detection and protection company has secured S$18.5 million in new contracts across Singapore and Malaysia, bringing its cumulative contract wins since January 2026 to more than S$147.7 million. The latest awards span infrastructure, marine and offshore, residential and industrial projects, including a Penang data centre project. Shares of Deluge closed 0.8 per cent or S$0.005 lower at S$0.605 on Tuesday.

data.title: Australiaâs jobless rate hits five-year high
data.description:
[SYDNEY] A second consecutive sharp fall in employment and an unexpected jump in the jobless rate to a five-year high raised concerns on Thursday (Nov 19) that the Australian economy may be headed for a sharper-than-expected slowdown as traders penciled in a rate cut for mid-2027.

Markets have now unwound expectations for any further tightening by the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) after its five increases this year took the cash rate to an 18-year high of 4.85 per cent, and are expecting rates to be cut at least once in the second half of next year.

The Australian Bureau of Statistics said that employment fell by 43,500 in October from September, when it dropped a revised 36,400, the biggest two-month total for job losses in five years.

The jobless rate climbed to 4.9 per cent, the highest since October 2021, from 4.7 per cent a month ago, reaching a level the RBA had not expected to see until the end of next year.

“These data place the RBA in a very tricky position,” said Andrew Ticehurst, senior economist at Nomura Australia. “It is still dealing with high inflation, which lags the economic cycle... However, it will also likely face growing criticism that it might have ‘overcooked’ the economy via tightening too much this year.”

The odds of a 25-basis-point rate cut at the RBA’s June 2027 meeting are seen at 68 per cent, market pricing indicated, rising to about 90 per cent for the August meeting. By the end of 2027, around 45 basis points of easing are priced in, double what had been expected before Thursday’s data.

That shift in sentiment hit the already pressured Australian dollar, which was down 0.5 per cent as it plumbed another 10-month low of US$0.6680. Three-year government bond futures rallied 17 ticks to 95.44, the highest since late August.

UBS, Nomura, the Commonwealth Bank of Australia (CBA) and the National Australia Bank are all tipping a rate cut in August next year, with stubbornly high inflation likely to keep the RBA on hold in the months ahead.

The October fall in the number of employed, which was driven mostly by losses in part-time jobs, was well below analysts’ forecast for a rise of around 25,000, while the jobless rate had been expected to hold steady at 4.7 per cent.

“Today’s data suggests the labour market is now at least back into balance but the risks have risen that we could see the labour market loosen further and faster than expected,” said Belinda Allen, head of Australian economics at the CBA.

“An on-hold decision in December is locked in for the RBA. February now feels an age away and the economy could be weaker by then if the labour market continues this way.”

Anecdotal evidence of a broader rise in layoffs is building, and the RBA board members who voted against a hike this month had flagged the risk the economy was facing a sharper-than-expected downturn.

Retailer David Jones will cut about 1,500 jobs after its collapse into administration, a union said on Wednesday, joining a string of job losses at Australian firms as the economy slows.

Thursday’s data also showed the participation rate dipped to 66.6 per cent, from 66.8 per cent, while hours worked fell 0.2 per cent. Youth unemployment – for people aged 15 to 24 – rose to 11.3 per cent in October, from 11.1 per cent, the highest in five years. REUTERS

data.title: Could Singapore equities take a sour turn in H1 2027? Hereâs what analysts say â and why
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The outlook on Singapore equities is looking mixed moving into the first half of 2027 – with Citi’s equity research team rating the Singapore market “underweight”, relative to benchmarks in the Asean bloc.

“The Straits Times Index (STI) is trading expensive not only relative to history, but even more so against Asean and Asia-Pacific peers,” the report by Citi issued on Wednesday (Nov 18) noted.

The Singapore benchmark hit an all-time peak of 5,801.96 on Sep 4, catalysed by shots of liquidity from the Equity Market Development Programme (EQDP) and surging interest in outperforming banks.

By Wednesday, it had lost over 12 per cent in just under 11 weeks to close at 5,054.89, after steep sell-offs sent local bank stocks diving from their earlier record levels, while tech stocks suffered from slipping confidence in the artificial intelligence trade.

According to Citi, the benchmark STI is now trading three standard deviations above the mean, compared with the MSCI Asean Index. It is also four standard deviations above the long-term mean of the FTSE Asean and FTSE Apac All-Cap indices.

The analysts set a target for the STI at 5,325, noting how positive catalysts are now “priced in” after years of outperformance, too.

They wrote: “The… banking sector – (worth) about 55 per cent of the STI – may struggle to drive market upside as dividend yield spreads compress to decade lows amid tightening net interest margins (NIMs), higher funding costs and softer wealth momentum.”

DBS is its only pick among banks with a “buy” rating, due to the counter’s 5 per cent yield and “better visibility on margins”.

The firm also recommended Sats , local telco Singtel , Yangzijiang Shipbuilding and CapitaLand Integrated Commercial Trust .

Francis Tan, Indosuez Wealth Management’s chief Asia strategist, reckoned the local banks are still important holdings for investors seeking earnings resilience and dividends – as they still have strong balance sheets and “diversified income streams”.

NIM outlook and valuations will increasingly matter more after a strong showing, however, he added.

For Maybank Securities however, OCBC is the preferred pick, due to “wealth integration and improving margins”, based on a Nov 10 report. It is “neutral” on Thailand, Vietnam and Indonesian markets – but “overweight” on Singapore.

Tan said: “Some Asean markets may offer stronger upside in a favourable global growth environment, but Singapore continues to provide a compelling combination of quality, dividends and relative resilience.”

SMID underperformance?

One key reason behind Citi’s downbeat outlook of the Singapore market in H1 next year is due to “waning” appetite for small and mid-caps (SMIDs) in the city-state.

It noted how the EQDP in 2025 helped fuel SMID performance, given its agenda to broaden market interest beyond large-cap stocks.

But that trend has since “reversed” in FY2026, according to the Citi analysts.

“Investors have de-rated SMIDs (over the last six months) and favoured large-cap names with the 20 largest stocks materially outperforming the next 80 stocks,” they wrote.

Charmaine Tan, research analyst at FSM Global, said investors should note how liquidity in many SMIDs remains “thin”, which can amplify price swings in both directions.

This is on top of how most EQDP funds launched in 2026; so their track records are still short.

“We expect returns from here to be driven less by broad rerating and more by companies delivering earnings growth. The Singapore Exchange found that the rerating since mid-2025 has been uneven, with valuation gains not always matching improvements in returns on equity, so selectivity remains important.”

The FSM Global analyst noted, however, how the recent sell-off has made entry valuations of SMIDs “more attractive” for investors to build positions in smaller companies. She is still constructive on Singapore equities going into 2027.

“For investors seeking SMID exposure, we (believe in) active strategies that can move across market capitalisations, holding established dividend payers alongside selected smaller companies with genuine earnings momentum, rather than relying on further policy-driven flows.”

The Citi analysts continued to stress how “weak” initial public offering performance would weigh further on SMIDs, with 82 per cent of FY2026 IPOs in Singapore being loss-making in the year to date.

“This may indicate fading optimism in EQDP’s benefits, especially expensive and crowded stocks,” they wrote.

However, recent STI weakness is beyond how EQDP measures have turned out, according to Indosuez Wealth Management’s Tan.

“The STI fell 5.3 per cent in October on a price-return basis. Technology, banks and shipyards were among the weaker sectors, while real estate investment trusts were relatively resilient,” he explained.

“That supports explaining the correction through sector performance and global risk sentiment, rather than treating it primarily as an EQDP disappointment.”

Moving forward, Tan is “cautiously constructive” on the Singapore market, and thinks there will be greater emphasis on stock selection.

“I think 2027 will be less about buying the entire Singapore market and more about identifying companies with sustainable earnings, (good) balance sheets and reasonable valuations,” he said.

data.title: Same AI price, very different costs: what to automate in South-east Asia
data.description:
A CUSTOMER opens a chat to dispute a charge. Resolving it takes a staff member about 20 minutes.

In Singapore, that costs the company about US$7.90. In Indonesia, it costs about US$0.60.

Yet, a leading customer service software firm charges the same price in both markets for an artificial intelligence agent to handle that chat.

Board members across South-east Asia are now asking their executive teams which workflows to hand to AI agents.

Our answer is that the business case depends on where the work is done. We compare the cost of the staff who do the work today with the cost of the AI that would do it instead.

The cost of a workflow

We cover six markets: Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Vietnam, the Philippines and Indonesia. Our staff costs are based on official wage data for clerical or similar roles, and a 50 per cent addition for employer contributions, supervision and tools.

One customer service software firm charges from US$0.99 each time its AI agent resolves a chat. But AI agents may not be fully autonomous in customer service, so our calculations factor in human staff costs.

The same software firm reports that its AI agent resolves three chats in four on average. Results vary widely by business, so we assume a more cautious scenario, where the AI resolves six chats in 10. Staff still handle the other four.

The human part of the job then moves from routine handling to reviewing and deciding. The staff checks one in 10 chats, taking three minutes each time.

For a business handling 20,000 chats a month, we assume half a full-time employee is required just to manage and maintain the agent.

By our calculations, at US$0.99 per outcome and even after a business pays for the staff it still needs, an AI agent cuts the cost of a chat in Singapore by about half.

In Malaysia, it cuts the cost by about a quarter, and in Thailand by about a tenth. In Vietnam, it saves nothing. In the Philippines and Indonesia, it adds to the cost.

These figures are illustrative estimates based on a single workflow and average wages, which mask wide variances between firms. In reality too, large clients often negotiate published prices down.

Our calculation also excludes the cost of building an agent, connecting it to existing systems and keeping it up to date as models change.

Businesses must therefore run the math using their own data.

The success rate matters too. If the agent resolves only half of all chats, the savings in Singapore fall to about 40 per cent.

If the agent resolves three in four, the savings rise to about 60 per cent. Singapore still saves the most and Indonesia still loses the most.

The reference firm charges for each chat its agent resolves. In higher-wage markets where staff cost more than about US$1 a chat, an agent with a higher resolution rate saves more money.

But where staff costs less, as in the Philippines and Indonesia, every extra chat the agent resolves actually adds to the cost.

The “build vs buy” variable

Some firms build their own agents rather than buy one from a vendor. For them, the choice of AI model matters a great deal.

For this scenario, we estimated costs for six leading models, based on their published prices. (Models we studied were Claude Sonnet 5.5, GPT-6 Astra, Gemini 3.8 Flash, GLM-5.2, DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Qwen 3.5.)

With the cheapest model, the self-built AI agent costs less than staff in every market. With the most expensive, it costs more everywhere except Singapore.

Engineering also makes a difference. When building an agent, design can directly affect the bottom line.

Take a mid-priced model: an agent that wastefully rereads twice as much company material at every step would lose its savings in Thailand, Vietnam, the Philippines and Indonesia.

An agent engineered to cache material, instead of rereading it, would pay off in all six markets.

Does running AI locally shift the case?

Today, most AI models run in a few giant data centres, mostly outside South-east Asia, and are sold at one global price.

As more countries insist on data sovereignty, keeping data and AI processing at home, more AI is likely to run locally. It would then carry local costs, including power and the cost of meeting each country’s rules and regulations.

Power is the easiest of these costs to measure. Electricity for a data centre costs about three times as much in Singapore as in Indonesia. Still, that makes the same AI only about 10 per cent more expensive.

By contrast, staff costs nearly 13 times as much. So even if AI runs locally, wages are likely to decide where AI agents make commercial sense. The cost of compliance is the open question.

Moving prices and looking beyond costs

Leading AI companies currently spend far more than they earn.

OpenAI expects to burn through about US$280 billion between 2026 and 2030, according to company projections reported by the Financial Times.

Prices may therefore rise. On our estimates, if a mid-priced model trebled its token prices, the savings from AI would disappear everywhere in South-east Asia except Singapore.

Exchange rates add a second risk. AI prices are set in US dollars. A weaker ringgit, baht, dong or rupiah makes the AI agent more expensive in local terms, while local salaries stay roughly the same.

Still, costs may not be the only consideration. AI agents work around the clock; they can absorb sudden peaks in demand, help launch new services faster and create new ways to serve customers.

Where an AI agent saves little in operating costs, these benefits could still justify deploying one.

What leaders should do

Start with the process. Map each workflow and remove unnecessary steps. Every step an AI agent performs adds cost.

Then ask three simple questions of each workflow: One, what does it cost us today? Two, what will it cost with an AI agent, including the staff it still needs? Three, how far could AI prices rise, or the local currency fall, before the business case fails?

Answer these questions separately for each market. Where the savings are small or negative, name the other benefits you expect in advance and measure them.

Crucially, businesses should keep the decision reversible for as long as possible.

Once teams are reshaped around AI agents, the know-how to do the work without them may be lost, and rebuilding that is slow and costly.

A phased roll-out is sensible. Each phase shows what the agent can handle before more of the workflow depends on it.

Avoid tying the workflow to a single provider or model. If that provider changes its terms, retires a model or fails, the business should be able to switch without starting over.

AI may cost the same in every market, but the case for it is won or lost, workflow by workflow and market by market.

Daniel Liebau is an adjunct associate professor with the Asian Institute of Digital Finance at the National University of Singapore, and the founding managing director of Lightbulb Capital, an innovation advisory firm. Damien Kopp is the founder and managing director of RebootUp, an AI advisory firm, and associate faculty, executive development, at Singapore Management University.

Workings are available from the authors on request.

data.title: US mortgage rates up for the first time in five weeks; housing starts rise
data.description:
US MORTGAGE rates rose for the first time in five weeks, halting a nascent rebound in home-purchase activity and clouding an already gloomy outlook for housing. Builders, meanwhile, started on more homes in October.

The contract rate on a 30-year fixed mortgage climbed 14 basis points to 7.37.35 per cent the week ended Nov 13, according to data released on Wednesday (Nov 18) by the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA).

The increase snaps a stretch of weekly declines that helped yield a modest pickup in home-purchase applications. Borrowing costs now stand nearly a full percentage point higher than a year ago.

An index of loan applications for home purchases slipped 2.5 per cent, marking the ninth weekly decline since the end of August. MBA’s refinance gauge fell 1.5 per cent, the first decrease in four weeks. 

A rapid escalation in financing costs in September into early October briefly brought mortgage rates to 7.5 per cent, punishing the housing market.

Contract signings in the home resale market reached a record low in September, and this month an index of home-builder sentiment fell to its lowest level in 14 years.

Multi-family dwellings up

Still, home-builders started more homes in October, driven largely by a rebound in apartment construction while the single-family market remained challenged by high mortgage rates.

Housing starts increased 9.9 per cent to an annualised rate of 1.31 million, the fastest in three months. Economists surveyed by Bloomberg expected a 1.25 million pace, based on the median projection. Those polled by Reuters, meanwhile, had forecast starts rising to a rate of 1.245 million units.

New construction of multi-family dwellings rose nearly 24 per cent. Starts of single-family homes increased 4 per cent to an annualised rate of 864,000.

Despite the October increase, the pace of single-family home construction remains near the slowest this year. Permits for houses slumped to the lowest since 2023, suggesting home-builders are waiting out a period of over-7 per cent mortgage rates and consumers’ worries about affordability.

Economists see the new-home market as stagnant at best until borrowing costs drop. The Federal National Mortgage Association, widely known as Fannie Mae, sees housing starts barely improving through at least the end of 2028.

“The US housing market is in a funk,” said Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union.

“Buyers don’t want to purchase a home at these high prices and high mortgage rates, and builders don’t want to build new homes or take risks in this market. This is a key reason home prices are staying high despite the lack of buyers.”

In an earnings call with analysts last month, builder PulteGroup noted its progress in reducing its share of “spec homes”, or homes built without a buyer in mind. Such homes can find quick buyers in strong market, but can require more sales incentives in slower times.

DR Horton, which targets many first-time buyers, is building more smaller homes lately, including duplexes and town houses.

Meanwhile, total building permits, which point to future construction, decreased 7.4 per cent last month to an annualised 1.3 million, the weakest since May 2020.

GDP impact

Once a solid contributor to the US’ economy, home construction has been a drag the last two years, weighing on gross domestic product for six of the past seven quarters.

Residential investment, which includes home-building, has contracted in eight of the last 10 quarters. Before the latest starts data, the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta’s GDPNow forecast showed residential investment may again subtract from growth in the fourth quarter.

By region, housing starts rose in the Midwest and the South. New construction in the South, the nation’s biggest home-building region, was the strongest since April. In the West, starts fell to the lowest level in more than six years.

The new residential construction data is volatile, and the government report showed 90 per cent confidence that the monthly change ranged from a 6.9 per cent decline to a 26.7 per cent gain.

“Builders are trying to unload current inventory heading into 2027, offering more incentives and lowering prices,” said Ben Ayers, senior economist at Nationwide.

“But with mortgage rates likely to remain elevated, activity could increasingly shift to apartments and condos with more renters staying in place due to housing affordability concerns.” BLOOMBERG, REUTERS

data.title: Singapore is winning the HQ race. Is it winning the leadership race?
data.description:
SINGAPORE now hosts about 1,030 foreign headquarters, up from roughly 770 in 2019. Over the same period, the resident professionals, managers and executives (PMEs) working in them grew by less than 8 per cent, from 12,700 to 13,700, as The Straits Times reported recently.

The explanation on offer is reassuring. A regional headquarters today, one adviser told the paper, is often “a leaner set-up focused on senior decision-making”, while operational roles move to cheaper markets.

That may well be true. The problem is that nobody measures it. Singapore counts its headquarters well. It does not yet count what they decide.

What the numbers miss

The PME figures also leave out foreign professionals, so headcount was never the right test of a headquarters. What matters is whether decision-making authority grew alongside the count. On that, the published figures are silent.

The Economic Strategy Review, published in June 2026, wants Singapore’s own companies to keep “headquarters, strategy and decision-making” functions here as they expand abroad, and foreign investors to make Singapore “a critical node” in their operations.

A headquarters, in the sense that counts for an economy, is where decisions are made. For a startup that re-domiciles here, that means where its chief executive and senior team sit.

Flipkart, founded in Bengaluru and serving customers across India, was incorporated in Singapore for 15 years before completing its move back to India in March 2026, ahead of a planned listing.

Throughout that time, Flipkart’s operations stayed in India alongside its executive leadership, while the Singapore headquarters focused on raising capital.

Grab offers a counter-example. Founded in Malaysia, the startup uses its Singapore headquarters as a control centre to manage localised teams across eight South-east Asian markets.

For a multinational’s regional headquarters, the test is narrower. In matrix organisations, few regional heads own every budget.

Even as global head offices hold ultimate control over bigger budgets, genuine regional headquarters can exert strategic influence and anchor a high-value ecosystem of professional services. For this, local leaders require sufficient autonomy.

Can the leaders here approve investment in the region, hire their own team and stop a project without needing a flight to the head office?

The Swiss mirror

Switzerland, where I am based, shows how control can move while the address stays.

Switzerland’s two federal technology universities, ETH in Zurich and EPFL in Lausanne, each produced a record number of new companies in 2025. But Swiss investors supplied at most about 13 per cent of later-stage capital for local startups that year, the Swiss Scale-Up Report 2026 found.

Growth money comes mostly from abroad.

Nexthink, an EPFL spin-off, is a Swiss success story. It still names Lausanne as one of its two headquarters. Its founder and chief executive, however, lives in the Boston area, and in October 2025, the company agreed to sell a majority stake to the American investor Vista Equity Partners.

On paper, Nexthink remains a Swiss-headquartered company. Where its biggest decisions are now taken is a different question.

That is also the risk Singapore faces: A company can maintain its official address in the country long after its true centre of decision-making has moved abroad.

When authority stays at home

In one executive search I handled, a company hired a Singapore-based leader for their understanding of the Asean market.

Yet headquarters, thousands of kilometres away, controlled the expansion budgets, assuming that what worked at home would work in the region.

The hire left for a direct competitor after 14 months, telling me that the lack of decision-making authority was the reason. The company had recruited local judgment but left it little room to act.

Retaining control overseas cost the company the local expertise it had recruited for its regional hub.

Singapore may get the leadership role, but does the authority move with it?

It can go the other way. In October 2026, Nike said the leadership team for a combined Asia-Pacific and Greater China region would be based in Singapore from fiscal year 2028, with some roles moving from its US headquarters.

Whether moves such as that bring real decision rights with them is exactly what Singapore should be tracking.

Closing the gap

Three changes would help.

First, measure authority as well as addresses. Singapore already counts its foreign headquarters and the resident PMEs in them. It could also survey whether those headquarters hold budget and hiring authority for the region, and publish the results in aggregate.

For startups that re-domicile, it could track where the chief executive and senior team are based.

Second, tie incentives to actual decision-making rights.

Today’s international headquarters award counts skilled jobs and local spending. Managing the group from Singapore is one qualifying activity among several, but it is not required.

As Singapore reviews its incentives for the era of the global minimum tax, awards could give weight to whether a regional chief executive or finance chief is a tax resident here and holds the regional budget.

Third, companies should move authority along with the address.

A startup that re-domiciles for capital or neutrality, while keeping every senior role elsewhere, has bought an address. A multinational that hires a regional leader here but signs off every budget at home has bought a title.

Businesses that put real decisions here, give regional leaders real budgets, and hire the next layer locally get what the address was meant to bring: proximity to regional customers, a deeper pool of talent and credibility with the investors who now concentrate their money here.

Singapore has already won the argument about where companies in this region want to be registered. The harder contest is about where they are run from.

To stay the region’s launchpad in 2027 and beyond, Singapore should count not only its headquarters, but also what they are allowed to decide.

The writer is the founder of Gunia Consulting, an advisory and executive search firm for organisation and leadership, with mandates in Europe and Asia, including Singapore. He is based in Zurich.

Views expressed here are his own. He used AI tools for research and editing before submitting the draft.

data.title: Nuclear arms and ending wars in Iran and Ukraine will top the agenda at Trump-Xi-Putin meeting
data.description:
[SHENZHEN] US President Donald Trump meets on Thursday (Nov 19) with China’s Xi Jinping and Russia’s Vladimir Putin, a moment that could mark a pivot in world history – or become a quickly forgotten photo op.

Trump, who will test his reputation as an expert dealmaker in the trilateral meeting, has promoted his time with Xi and Putin – two of America’s leading rivals – as a chance to hash out rules for controlling nuclear arms and to start resolving the wars in Ukraine and Iran. Experts have kept expectations low for major breakthroughs.

Trump had a separate one-on-one meeting with Xi – his third substantial meeting with him this year – right before the trilateral.

The US president praised their friendship and their shared interest in having oil shipped through the Strait of Hormuz, which has become a key site of attacks in the Iran war. Trump suggested he would push Xi to buy more agricultural products from America.

“I’ll be asking you to do some more for our farmers,” Trump said.

Xi said that Trump’s efforts “will be recorded in history” and that he was committed to working with the US president, according to a translation.

Trump also added a separate sit-down with Putin to his schedule, marking the first time the leaders have held talks since their discussions in Alaska last year that failed to broker a deal to ease Russia’s war in Ukraine.

“Wonderful things can come out of this – or at least start,” Trump said after joining Putin for the one-on-one meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) Summit, calling Putin “my friend.”

“We’ve had a great relationship for many years,” Trump said after shaking hands with Putin. Their meeting together lasted roughly 40 minutes.

Trump has frequently boasted of his rapport with Putin, even as relations between the US and Ukraine appear to have cratered recently.

Trump rejected new Russia sanctions, while Kyiv was undermined by disruptions in satellite support for its drones during the war.

Along for the trip – but so far keeping a low profile – is Elon Musk, whose company SpaceX has intermittently throttled the military-grade Starshield satellite system used by Ukraine for launching its drones and intercepting hits from Russia.

One meeting is unlikely to produce a breakthrough in nuclear talks

Trump has said he wants to talk to the leaders about their nuclear stockpiles.

The last nuclear arms pact between Russia and the US, known as New START, expired in February, and Trump has said he wants “a new, improved and modernised” deal that includes China.

But China has less motivation to accept limits given that its arsenal of more than 600 warheads is far smaller than the more than 5,000 warheads believed to be in each of the US and Russian stockpiles.

Daryl Kimball, executive director of the Arms Control Association, said Trump’s showmanship could at best start a process that would eventually lead to a sustained set of talks for reducing nuclear arsenals.

“We need more than diplomatic theater and photo opportunities between Xi, Putin and Trump at Apec,” Kimball said. “And one meeting will not likely produce dramatic breakthroughs.”

Trump told Fox News in his interview that “it’s a very hard thing to do” to ask a leader to reduce nuclear stockpiles.

Trump boasts about his relationships. But the ties between Xi and Putin are stronger

Putin’s foreign affairs adviser Yuri Ushakov told reporters that Putin, Trump and Xi would likely touch on the war in Ukraine, though the agenda was not fully set. Trump has said he wants to discuss that war – as well as the conflict in Iran.

His ambitions recall an era of great power politics when wealthier countries felt entitled to decide the fate of seemingly lesser nations.

Trump is negotiating with China and Russia without the involvement of Ukraine – or countries like Germany, France, the United Kingdom, Japan and South Korea that also have stakes in the outcome of any talks.

The US president has openly pursued a Nobel Peace Prize even as he took military action against Venezuela and Iran.

He also threatened earlier this year to take Greenland by force from Denmark, a gambit that led to an agreement for the construction of US military bases.

Trump has long believed his ability to create personal connections gives him a diplomatic edge. Xi appealed to his ego on Wednesday by greeting Air Force One on the airport tarmac, as the two leaders turned their handshake into a one-armed hug.

But Trump does not appear to always have the same deep relationship based on common interests that Xi and Putin share. For all the compliments the US president has showered on the two autocrats, the warmth has not always been mutually effusive.

On Wednesday at Apec, Xi greeted Putin by calling him “my old friend”.

The Russian leader responded by declaring Xi to be his “dear friend”. China has helped economically support Russia after its 2022 invasion of Ukraine, providing Putin with a financial lifeline after the US and its allies imposed new sanctions.

“China-Russia relations have remained steadfast through storms while taking a long-term view,” Xi said to Putin. “They have brought greater stability and certainty to a world marked by intertwined changes and turbulence.”

The pair discussed the war in Ukraine during their talks, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told Russian state news agency RIA Novosti.

By contrast, when Xi came to the White House for a state visit in September, he was far more restrained with Trump, saying they had built a “personal rapport and stayed in touch”.

Trump and Xi plan to meet a total of four times this year, with their final time together coming in December at the G20 summit being held at the Trump National Doral Golf Club in Florida.

Ukraine and its European allies are suspicious of the trilateral meeting that could potentially cut them out of the process.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has said Europeans feared another “Anchorage moment”, a reference to last year’s Putin-Trump meeting in Alaska that produced proposals that were rejected by Ukraine and its partners.

Conflicts on AI and trade also hang over the meetings

While Trump views his relationship with China as a positive, it has not necessarily resulted in meaningful changes between the world’s two largest economies.

China continues to run large trade surpluses with the rest of the world, while the US has almost equally large trade deficits.

And the race between the US and China to master artificial intelligence has grown tense over the past two weeks.

Trump ally Jensen Huang resigned last week as the CEO of Nvidia after confessing to an extramarital affair with a woman, Alice Huang, whose company helped to give China access to the company’s advanced computer chips used to develop AI models.

Beijing has denied that Alice Huang was a Chinese government agent.

Trump held off on imposing tougher restrictions on China’s ability to access the chips, suggesting he did not want to insult China and aggravate relations.

Before Apec, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer met with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng.

The US officials said afterward that China had not fully honoured its commitments made last year in a Trump-Xi meeting to buy more US agricultural products and loosen restrictions on the sale of rare earth minerals needed for electronics.

The trade truce between the US and China reached last year after dueling tariff hikes is set to expire by Jan 10 next year.

Trump officials have dangled the possibility of opening up highly sanctioned trade with Russia as an incentive for ending hostilities in Ukraine, and Trump has frequently demonstrated that he sees trade as a foreign policy tool.

Meanwhile, both China and Russia have used trade to support Iran, even during the US war on that country, which has pushed up energy prices and reduced global economic growth. AP

data.title: Founder of Singapore-listed MindChamps seeks A$100 million for first pre-school fund
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The founder of Singapore-listed MindChamps PreSchool has launched an investment platform that is seeking to raise A$100 million (US$66.7 million) for its first fund to acquire and develop purpose-built pre-school properties in Australia.

The platform, MindFunds, will pursue investments across the education sector, David Chiem, founder of MindChamps, a franchiser of pre-school centres, said in an interview.

The firm has sold 45 franchise licences as part of its expansion in Australia, and the fund will acquire or develop properties where franchisees can open and operate their centres, he said.

MindChamps is targeting a first close for the fund in the first half of 2027, according to Goh Seh Harn, chief executive officer of Trigger Asset Management, who advises on the fund. It also plans a follow-on fund of A$500 million, he said.

Across Asia, growing demand for quality education has fuelled a rush of private capital into schools, opening up new sources of funding for a sector that has traditionally relied on equity and bank loans.

Financiers such as Apollo Global Management and KKR & Co have bought stakes and lent money to school chains, betting that rising incomes and families’ willingness to spend more on their children will fuel expansion.

MindChamps operates pre-schools, after-school care centres and therapy services for children. The Singapore-based firm company has also expanded its presence into markets including Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines and Myanmar. BLOOMBERG

data.title: Stocks to watch: Yangzijiang Shipbuilding, Seatrium, Frencken
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Thursday (Nov 19):

Yangzijiang Shipbuilding : The shipbuilder’s subsidiary has entered into an investment agreement with China’s Taicang Port Economic and Technological Development Zone. The agreement is in relation to a project to develop a clean energy vessel intelligent manufacturing base in Taicang city, located in Jaingsu province. The group expects capital expenditure for the project to be about 3.38 billion yuan (US$507 million). Shares of Yangzijiang Shipbuilding ended 1.6 per cent or S$0.07 higher at S$4.39 on Wednesday, before the announcement.

Seatrium : The offshore, marine and energy specialist reported that its net order book stood at S$12.2 billion as at end-September, comprising 35 projects with deliveries extending through 2033. It had secured S$1.7 billion in new orders so far this year. Seatrium expects its underlying net profit for FY2026 to be materially higher than in FY2025. The counter ended 0.6 per cent or S$0.01 lower at S$1.71, before the news.

Frencken : The technology manufacturer announced on Wednesday (Nov 18) a 31.3 per cent year-on-year increase in earnings to S$13 million for its third quarter ended Sep 30. Revenue grew 12.8 per cent to S$238.5 million, from S$211.5 million a year earlier. The increase was mainly driven by Frencken’s mechatronics division’s revenue, which rose 13.4 per cent to S$214.3 million. The counter ended S$0.01, or 0.6 per cent, up at S$1.71 before the news.

data.title: Indonesia passes long-awaited asset forfeiture law after 18-year wait
data.description:
[JAKARTA] Indonesia’s parliament on Thursday (Nov 19) passed a long-awaited asset forfeiture bill, marking a significant step in the government’s bid to recover assets linked to corruption and other financial crimes.

The legislation, which has been under discussion for 18 years, is intended to strengthen law enforcement by allowing authorities to confiscate proceeds of crime and return them to the state or victims, including those affected by large-scale investment fraud.

Among the law’s key provisions is a mechanism known as non-conviction-based asset forfeiture. It allows authorities to pursue the confiscation of assets linked to criminal activities without first securing a criminal conviction, under certain circumstances and subject to judicial proceedings.

The legislation covers corruption and a range of other offences, including narcotics trafficking, terrorism financing, human trafficking and large-scale fraud involving information technology.

It also provides a mechanism for compensating victims of fraudulent investment schemes and illegal share trading, who have often struggled to recover their money through existing legal processes.

Under the framework, victims could receive compensation directly from the proceeds of assets sold after being confiscated from perpetrators, rather than having the recovered funds transferred to the state without necessarily reaching those affected.

The bill spent nearly two decades stalled amid political resistance and disagreements over the scope of the state’s powers to seize assets, particularly concerns that the mechanism could be abused to target individuals or businesses without sufficient legal safeguards.

Habiburokhman, a member of parliament, described the passage as the culmination of an 18-year legislative process and a long-awaited response to public demands for stronger action against corruption.

“This is good news for victims of investment scam and illegal stocks trading,” Habiburokhman said, according to local media reports.

The final version of the bill has yet to be made publicly available, as the text is typically released to the public only in the week following its passage.

Corruption has long been a major governance challenge in South-east Asia’s largest economy, affecting public procurement, infrastructure projects and the management of state resources.

Lawmakers and the government completed deliberations at the committee level on Wednesday, before the bill was endorsed at the plenary session on Thursday chaired by House Speaker Puan Maharani.

While Indonesia has prosecuted numerous high-profile corruption cases, recovering illicit wealth has often proved difficult, particularly when assets are concealed through complex ownership structures or transferred to third parties.

The legislation’s passage comes amid mounting public pressure on the government and parliament to strengthen accountability and address governance concerns.

Public frustration over corruption and economic grievances has spilled onto the streets, with protests putting pressure on lawmakers to respond to demands for greater transparency and stronger enforcement.

The law also provides for the management of confiscated assets, including their storage, maintenance, use and eventual sale, with oversight intended to ensure transparency and accountability.
